title: Smt. Rekha Chahar v. State of U.P. and 2 Others
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
coram: Surya Prakash Kesarwani and Jayant Banerji, JJ. (final order disposing of the writ, 18.01.2023); earlier interim orders by several other Division Benches - incl. Manoj Kumar Gupta and Dr. Yogendra Kumar Srivastava, JJ. (15.07.2022) and Siddhartha Varma and Vipin Chandra Dixit, JJ. (22.12.2022)
disposition: An order-sheet writ in which the petitioner, who had applied on 09.01.2022 for a 2 KW residential connection, challenged the demand of Rs.48,204 raised as the cost of enhancing an overloaded distribution transformer by 16 KVA before releasing her connection. Across successive orders the Division Bench repeatedly required the Executive Engineer to justify the demand - to disclose the total transformer load, the cost of augmentation, the basis of the Rs.48,204 figure, and whether that cost was to be borne by the petitioner alone or by all consumers - and to disclose the specific provision of the Supply Code, tariff order, rules or Government Orders authorising it; by order dated 22.12.2022 it recorded that it was 'absolutely not satisfied' with the affidavits, which did not show how the licensee's duty under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 had been fulfilled or why an applicant for a fresh connection was being charged for transformer augmentation. It also warned (15.07.2022) that a demand raised in violation of law would be treated as sheer harassment warranting a recommendation for disciplinary proceedings. By the final order dated 18.01.2023, without expressing any opinion on merits, the Court disposed of the writ by relegating the petitioner to a fresh representation before respondent no. 2, to be decided in accordance with law within four weeks.
headnote: The petitioner, Smt. Rekha Chahar, applied on 09.01.2022 for a 2 KW (2 KVA) permanent residential electricity connection, depositing the process fee; the connection was withheld on the ground that the distribution transformer was already overloaded and its capacity had to be increased by 16 KVA, for which the petitioner was required to deposit Rs.48,204. In a series of orders on the order-sheet, the Division Bench pressed the Executive Engineer to justify the demand - to disclose on affidavit the total load on the transformer, the total cost of augmentation, how the figure of Rs.48,204 was arrived at, and whether that cost was to be borne by the petitioner alone or by all consumers - and to identify the specific provision of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, the tariff order, the rules or Government Orders under which the charge was demanded. Finding the department's successive affidavits wanting, the Court (22.12.2022) recorded that it was 'absolutely not satisfied' and that the affidavits did not show how the licensee's duty under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 of the Supply Code had been fulfilled or why an applicant seeking a fresh connection was being charged for enhancing the transformer load; earlier (15.07.2022) it had warned that if the demand were found to violate the law it would be treated as sheer harassment, exposing the responsible officer to a recommendation for disciplinary proceedings. These, however, were interim observations: by the final order dated 18.01.2023 (Surya Prakash Kesarwani and Jayant Banerji, JJ.), without expressing any opinion on merits, the Court disposed of the writ by giving the petitioner liberty to submit a fresh representation before respondent no. 2 within three weeks, to be decided in accordance with law within four weeks.
facts: The petitioner, Smt. Rekha Chahar, a resident of House No. 26, Gangotri Vihar-Rohta, Gwalior Road, District Agra, applied on 09.01.2022 for a permanent 2 KW residential electricity connection (from the feeder at Bad, District Agra), depositing the process fee. The connection was not released; the petitioner was told that the distribution transformer was already overloaded, that its capacity had to be enhanced by 16 KVA, and that she must deposit Rs.48,204 towards that cost. She filed WRIT-C No. 19481 of 2022 seeking a mandamus to provide the connection and to decide her representation dated 15.05.2022. By order dated 15.07.2022 the Division Bench called for a personal affidavit of respondent no. 2 disclosing the total transformer load, the cost of augmentation, the basis of the Rs.48,204 demand, and whether that cost was to be borne by the petitioner alone or by all consumers, and left it open to respondent no. 2 to re-examine and, if the demand was unjustified, to release the connection; it also warned that a demand in violation of law would be treated as harassment. The department's affidavits were found inadequate (23.09.2022: the relevant provisions of law were not disclosed; 22.12.2022: the affidavits did not show how the duty under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 was fulfilled, and the Court was 'absolutely not satisfied'). The matter passed through several Benches; finally, on 18.01.2023 (Surya Prakash Kesarwani and Jayant Banerji, JJ.), the Court disposed of the writ by relegating the petitioner to a fresh representation before respondent no. 2, to be decided in accordance with law within four weeks.

reusable_constructions.construction: An applicant for a fresh electricity connection cannot be saddled with the cost of enhancing/augmenting the distribution transformer's capacity unless the licensee discloses the legal basis for the charge; augmentation of the distribution system is prima facie the licensee's duty under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and whether the cost falls on the single applicant or is spread over all consumers must be justified.

An authority demanding a charge for an electricity connection must disclose the specific provision of law - the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, the tariff order, the rules or Government Orders - authorising the demand; repeated failure to disclose the legal basis leaves the demand unsupported.
A demand raised in violation of law may be treated as sheer harassment, exposing the responsible officer to a recommendation for disciplinary proceedings.

Where the justification for an impugned demand remains unexamined, the writ court may relegate the applicant to a fresh representation before the competent authority to be decided in accordance with law within a fixed time, without expressing any opinion on merits.

holding_units.clause: 4.1 r/w 4.2 - licensee's duty to supply; cost of augmenting the distribution transformer for a fresh connection
holding_units.topic: Applicant for a fresh connection prima facie not to be charged for augmenting the transformer capacity without the licensee justifying the demand under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2
holding_units.question: Can an applicant for a fresh electricity connection be required to bear the cost (here Rs.48,204) of enhancing the capacity of an overloaded distribution transformer, and is that consistent with the licensee's duty under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005?
holding_units.holding: The Court did not finally decide, but expressed strong prima facie disapproval. It repeatedly required the licensee to justify demanding Rs.48,204 from a single applicant for augmenting the transformer, including whether that cost should be borne by the petitioner alone or by all consumers, and recorded (22.12.2022) that it was 'absolutely not satisfied' with the affidavits, which did not show how the licensee's duty under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 of the Supply Code had been fulfilled or why money was being demanded from an applicant seeking a fresh connection for enhancement of the transformer load. These were interim observations; the writ was ultimately disposed of by relegating the petitioner to a representation before respondent no. 2, without a decision on merits.

evidence.quote: whether the amount to be spent in enhancing the capacity is to be borne by the petitioner alone or by all consumers.

From the two affidavits which the Electricity Department had filed it is not clear as to how the duty cast upon the licensee had been fulfilled under the Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

Let a further affidavits be filed of the Executive Engineer, respondent No.2 to explain why despite the provisions contained in Clauses 4.1 and 4.2 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, money is being demanded from the petitioner for the enhancement of the transformer load.

holding_units.flag: Compilation of order-sheets (15.07.2022-18.01.2023) with no printed page numbers and no numbered paragraphs; pins reference the order dates. The Clauses 4.1/4.2 observations are prima facie/interim - the final order of 18.01.2023 relegated the petitioner to a representation without deciding the merits (see not_decided).

holding_units.clause: 4.2 and general law - authority must disclose the specific legal provision authorising a connection charge
holding_units.topic: A charge demanded for a connection must be traceable to a disclosed provision of the Code, tariff order, rules or Government Orders
holding_units.question: Must the licensee, when demanding a charge as a condition of a new connection, disclose the specific provision of law authorising the demand, and what follows from a failure to do so?
holding_units.holding: Yes. The Court required the respondents to disclose the relevant provisions of the U.P. Electricity Code, the tariff order, the rules or Government Orders under which the Rs.48,204 charge was demanded, noting that the affidavit filed did not disclose the relevant provisions of law under which the charges had been demanded. On the department's repeated failure to disclose the legal basis, the Court was left 'absolutely not satisfied' with the affidavits. This was an interim view; the merits were not decided.

evidence.quote: In the affidavit, the relevant provisions of law under which those charges have been demanded have not been disclosed.
disclosing the relevant provisions of U.P. Electricity Code or the tariff order or the relevant rules or Government Orders under which the charges are being demanded from the petitioner.
we are absolutely not satisfied with the affidavits which have been filed.

principle_tags.application: A 2 KW applicant was asked to pay Rs.48,204 to augment an overloaded transformer; the Court was 'absolutely not satisfied' that the licensee had shown, consistently with its duty under Clauses 4.1 and 4.2, why the applicant alone should bear the augmentation cost.

The Court repeatedly required the department to disclose the specific provisions of the Code, tariff order, rules or Government Orders authorising the Rs.48,204 demand; the successive affidavits' failure to do so left the demand unsupported.

The Court warned that if the impugned demand were found to violate any provision of law it would be treated as sheer harassment, compelling a recommendation for disciplinary proceedings against the person responsible.

not_decided.point: Whether the demand of Rs.48,204 for enhancing the transformer capacity is legally sustainable and whether the petitioner is entitled to the 2 KW connection
not_decided.note: Not decided on merits despite strong prima facie observations; by the final order dated 18.01.2023 the Court, without expressing any opinion on merits, relegated the petitioner to a fresh representation before respondent no. 2, to be decided in accordance with law within four weeks.

related_cases.note: Kitab Shree - Clauses 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4 oblige the licensee to consider a new-connection application and, if there is no legal impediment, to grant it speedily, the duty the licensee was pressed to honour here.
Sneha Devi - Clause 4.1 obliges the licensee to supply within one month of a completed application, the timeframe/duty against which the withholding of the petitioner's connection was tested.

Smt. Meenu Singh - a new connection refused under Clause 4.1 for an extraneous ground (arrears of other occupants) drew a prima facie interim observation that the refusal was impermissible, mirroring the interim posture and extraneous-demand concern here.

Smt. Soni Dwivedi - marks the boundary of Clause 4.1: a new connection may lawfully be refused only for a recognised legal impediment (there, the premises' arrears), in contrast to the unexplained augmentation charge questioned here.
